claims.text: Adding a low concentration of yttrium improves the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Adding a low concentration of yttrium increases the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without yttrium.
The proposed yttrium concentration is approximately 1–5 at.%.
The comparison should use alloys arc-melted under inert atmosphere and rapidly solidified by melt spinning.
Thermal stability should be assessed by DSC at approximately 10 K/min in nitrogen over the range from Tg to Tx.
Yttrium promotes atomic-packing frustration in the alloy.
Yttrium stabilizes specific local bonding configurations with phosphorus.
The proposed packing frustration and local Y–P bonding configurations impede crystallization kinetics.
Yttrium addition increases atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Yttrium addition increases chemical short-range order in the alloy.
The increased atomic-size mismatch and chemical short-range order increase the critical cooling rate needed for crystallization.
The proposed structural changes raise the onset temperature of crystallization.
Yttrium addition slows atomic mobility during thermal annealing.
Yttrium addition suppresses nucleation events during thermal annealing.
The yttrium-modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the baseline alloy.
The yttrium-modified alloy will exhibit a higher crystallization onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy without yttrium has a lower Tx and requires a higher cooling rate to become amorphous.
The benefit occurs only within an optimal yttrium range of approximately 1–5 at.%.
The benefit may not occur for substantially different alloy compositions or processing routes that do not establish the proposed atomic-scale interactions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the intervention increases a 'critical cooling rate needed for crystallization,' whereas the predicted outcome says it lowers the critical cooling rate for glass formation. The critical-cooling-rate terminology is used with inconsistent direction and must be defined consistently.
